title: First CRUD Application in ASP.NET Core MVC
description: Build a complete Create, Read, Update, and Delete application in ASP.NET Core MVC using a static repository, tag helpers, model binding, and data validation.

data.text: In this lesson you will build a complete **CRUD** (Create, Read, Update, Delete) application for managing employee records. You will use a static C# class as an in-memory repository — no database required — so you can focus entirely on how the MVC pieces fit together.
What Are CRUD Operations?
CRUD is the foundation of most web applications. Every operation on data falls into one of these four categories:
Step 1 — Create the Project
Open a terminal and create a new MVC project called `FirstApp`:

data.title: Create the Project
data.content: Scaffold a new ASP.NET Core MVC project.
data.code:
dotnet new mvc -n FirstApp
cd FirstApp

data.text: Run `dotnet run` to confirm the template app launches without errors before proceeding.
Step 2 — Create the Model and Repository
Create a `Models` folder if it doesn't already exist. Inside it, add two files: `Employee.cs` (the data model) and `Repository.cs` (an in-memory static store).

data.title: Models/Employee.cs
data.content: The data model representing an employee record.

data.title: Models/Repository.cs
data.content: A static in-memory repository that behaves like a simple database.

data.title: Why a Static Repository?
data.text: A static `List<T>` persists for the lifetime of the running application. It behaves like a simple database — data survives across HTTP requests but is lost when the app stops. This is perfect for learning CRUD without setting up SQL Server.
Step 3 — Create the EmployeeController
Add a new controller called `EmployeeController` inside the `Controllers` folder. It will contain all four CRUD action methods.

data.title: Controllers/EmployeeController.cs
data.content: The full controller skeleton with Read (Index) and Create (GET + POST) actions.

ASP.NET Core automatically maps form field names to model properties, so the Employee parameter is populated for free.

data.caption: The complete CRUD request lifecycle in the EmployeeController.
data.definition:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Read
        B1["GET /Employee/Index"] --> B2["return View(AllEmployees)"]
    end
    subgraph Create
        C1["GET /Employee/Create"] --> C2["return View()"]
        C3["POST /Employee/Create"] --> C4{ModelState.IsValid?}
        C4 -->|Yes| C5["Repository.Create(employee)"]
        C4 -->|No| C6["return View()"]
        C5 --> C7["return View('Thanks', employee)"]
    end
    subgraph Update
        D1["GET /Employee/Update?empname=X"] --> D2["find employee, return View"]
        D3["POST /Employee/Update"] --> D4{ModelState.IsValid?}
        D4 -->|Yes| D5["update fields, RedirectToAction('Index')"]
    end
    subgraph Delete
        E1["POST /Employee/Delete?empname=X"] --> E2["Repository.Delete(employee)"]
        E2 --> E3["RedirectToAction('Index')"]
    end

data.text: Step 6 — Add Model Validations

Right now a user can submit the form with empty fields. Add validation rules using **Data Annotation** attributes on the `Employee` model so the framework validates automatically during model binding.

data.title: Models/Employee.cs (with Validation)
data.content: Employee model decorated with validation attributes.

data.text: The `` elements in the form views will automatically display error messages next to each field when validation fails. You already added these in the Create and Update views.

data.title: ModelState.IsValid Guards Your Data
data.text: Always wrap your POST action logic in `if (ModelState.IsValid) { ... }`. If validation fails, the framework automatically re-renders the form with error messages — no extra code needed.

data.text: Run and Test the Application
Run `dotnet run` and navigate to `/Employee/Create`. Fill in the form and submit — you should land on the Thanks page. Click "View All Employees" to see the list, then test Update and Delete.

data.title: Test Validation
data.text: Try submitting the form with an empty Name field or an Age below 16. The validation messages should appear inline and the record should not be saved.

data.title: Exercise: Extend the CRUD App
data.description: Add new features to deepen your understanding of the MVC request cycle.
steps: Add a search feature: create a text box on the Index page and an `[HttpPost] Search(string query)` action that filters employees by name.
Add a `[HttpGet] Details(string empname)` action that shows a read-only details view for one employee.
Add a confirmation step before deleting: create a `DeleteConfirmed` GET action that shows a confirmation page, then the POST action performs the deletion.
data.expectedOutcome: You have a working search, a details page, and a safe two-step delete confirmation flow.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: CRUD stands for Create, Read, Update, and Delete — the four fundamental data operations.
A static List<T> repository is a simple alternative to a database for learning purposes.
Each CRUD operation typically needs a GET action (show the form/page) and a POST action (process the submission).
asp-for, asp-validation-for, and asp-action tag helpers reduce boilerplate and prevent broken links.
ModelState.IsValid is the gatekeeper: only save or update data when all validations pass.
CSS in wwwroot/css/site.css applies globally to all views.
data.takeaway: You now have a fully working CRUD application. Understanding this pattern is essential — almost every real web application you build will be a variation of CRUD.
